title: Downtown Guelph heritage district designated
subtitle: Draft downtown planning permit by-law heard, Hanlon Creek Business Park housekeeping changes, and heritage notices and a Baker Street rezoning.
overview: Council designated the Downtown Guelph Heritage Conservation District and adopted its district plan {{vote:m8}}. The plan sets heritage permit rules for the original downtown core. Staff said it has no application fee for heritage permits, sets expected turnaround times, and welcomes sustainability and accessibility upgrades.

Council also heard a statutory public meeting on a draft Downtown Community Planning Permit By-law and received the report {{vote:m6}}. No decision was made. The draft would replace downtown zoning, combine several approvals into one process and require affordable housing in exchange for added height. Developers questioned whether the requirement is viable. Staff will meet with them, review the numbers and return, possibly later than March.

Council approved housekeeping changes for Hanlon Creek Business Park Phase 3, including mapping corrections, a new block for a possible municipal water well, and a draft plan extension to November 8, 2029 {{vote:m7}}. Through the consent report, council also approved a rezoning for two mixed-use towers at 55 Baker Street and 152 and 160 Wyndham Street North, and several heritage property decisions {{vote:m1}}.

decisions.detail: Council designated the downtown district by by-law and adopted the district plan that guides changes to properties within it.
Council received the report on the draft downtown planning permit by-law after the statutory public meeting, with no approval at this stage.

decisions.item: Hanlon Creek Business Park Phase 3 amendments
decisions.detail: Council approved Official Plan and zoning map corrections, a three-year draft plan extension to November 8, 2029, and a new block for a municipal water well.

decisions.item: 55 Baker, 152 and 160 Wyndham St N rezoning
decisions.detail: Council approved a site-specific Downtown 1 zoning change to allow two mixed-use towers of 17 and 19 storeys with about 401 homes.
The City Clerk was authorized to publish notice of intention to designate the property under the Ontario Heritage Act.

debate: Delegates for a downtown developer said the affordable housing requirement on height above the current zoning would make their project unworkable. They said a 5% requirement would work, and they questioned the economic analysis behind the 33% figure.

Delegates argued that the by-law treats neighbouring sites unequally, because sites with existing height rights face no requirement. They also said the complete community charge plus the affordable housing requirement amounts to two charges on one property.

Staff said the added height is a large increase in value and that an affordable housing requirement is the only tool available for it. They said the financial analysis was meant to be prototypical and pointed to the city's affordable housing strategy. Staff committed to meeting the developers who wrote in and reporting back.

Councillors asked staff to review the numbers with developers, reconsider the affordable housing requirement and consider exemptions or phasing for projects already in progress. Another asked whether the by-law gives staff too little delegated authority at the class two level. Staff said they would review the limits.
On the heritage district, councillors said it balances conservation with growth and addresses insurance and accessibility concerns. No delegations spoke.
